proposals.relationship: Davis disputes Williams’s economic-decline explanation of British abolition while explicitly separating it from slavery’s contribution to industrialization.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2012 reply to Barbara Solow, whose contrary evidence and defense remain explicit in the exchange. Davis limits his repudiation to the decline/abolition hypothesis and credits Williams for initiating the debate; his strong consensus language is his assessment, not the atlas’s final verdict. Williams1944, Ryden and the cited economic histories remain unread.
primary_locators: NYRB12January2012, Solow letter and complete Davis reply, especially opening distinction, Fogel/Engerman/Drescher resources and final credit to Williams.

proposals.relationship: Genovese’s analysis of slaveholding social relations and ideology supplies a resource in Davis’s account of slavery and abolition.
proposals.evidence_note: Davis1995 explicitly finds the Genovese/Fox-Genovese case convincing; their credit remains shared. Sinha2019pp152–153 separately identifies Genovese’s influence on the1975 Age of Revolution and their conversations as fellows. Named mediation for that earlier transmission, not fresh reading of either1970s book. Sinha’s speculative reverse Hegel transmission is not accepted. This resource coexists with Davis’s specific1995criticism.
primary_locators: Davis1995 opening discussion from Marxist sensitivity through the paragraph crediting both Genovese and Elizabeth Fox-Genovese; Sinha2019pp152–153, transition across the page on Genovese’s influence and Stanford conversations.

proposals.relationship: Davis values Genovese’s recovery of Southern thought but questions his political alliance with conservatism and his treatment of the liberal tradition.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1995review, concluding objection: Davis invokes liberal critics of human perfectibility and argues that dismantling public power can serve corporate interests. Praise of scholarship and shared concerns about market values remain explicit. These are Davis’s political/intellectual judgments about the three reviewed books, not an editorial judgment of Genovese’s whole career; books unread.
primary_locators: Southern Comfort, final block beginning It is no doubt true through the final sentence on private/public bigness; earlier paragraphs identify the scholarship Davis values.

proposals.relationship: Foner praises Davis’s trilogy but questions speculative psychological dehumanization and notes that the book’s fugitive-slave evidence challenges its generalization.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2014review distinguishes racial dehumanization as a legal/social practice from claims of internalized psychological damage. Foner values Davis’s treatment of free Black leadership and contingency while making this objection. The criticism targets the2014volume’s argument; no dismissal of the trilogy or whole-book reading claimed.
primary_locators: The Nation,29January2014online/17February2014issue: paragraphs on psychological implications/Elkins/Freudian explanation and the later fugitive-slave discussion beginning Davis devotes a revealing chapter.

proposals.relationship: In Garrett Epps’s reading, Davis adapts Hofstadter’s paranoid-style concept to antebellum Slave Power arguments.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation, Epps2004p186, not fresh reading of Davis1969 or Hofstadter. Epps also criticizes Davis for conflating fringe conspiracy claims with sober constitutional arguments; his objection remains attributed and is held for missing Epps endpoint. A bounded conceptual resource, not endorsement of the diagnosis of abolitionists.
primary_locators: Garrett Epps, The Antebellum Political Background of the Fourteenth Amendment, Law and Contemporary Problems67(2004),p186 and notes81–84; PDFpage12.

proposals.relationship: Sinha identifies Weber’s Protestant Ethic as a model for Davis’s chapter on the Quaker ethic and antislavery international.
proposals.evidence_note: Named Sinha2019reading atp153; she differentiates humble early Quaker dissenters from the later capitalist-elite emphasis and criticizes the latter. This is her identified model, not a primary Davis acknowledgment; Weber1905 and Davis1975chapter5 remain unread. No claim that Weber alone supplied the argument.
primary_locators: Sinha2019printedp153, paragraph beginning The most obvious model through the ensuing Quaker-values discussion; chapter5 title explicit.

proposals.relationship: Sinha reads Davis’s account of British antislavery’s social function as an application of Gramsci’s ideological-hegemony concept.
proposals.evidence_note: Named Sinha2019p154 and note35(bookp379); she distinguishes Genovese’s slaveholder application, Davis’s British limit and Ashworth’s American extension while criticizing the explanatory consequences. Original Davis and Gramsci passages remain unread; no wholesale Marxist-school affiliation or agreement with Sinha inferred.
primary_locators: Sinha2019printedp154, paragraph beginning Genovese had appropriated Antonio Gramsci through Davis’s British limitation and Ashworth distinction; note35.

proposals.relationship: Faust places Davis’s linking of ideas, institutions and social action among the slavery histories that redirected her generation’s research.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2014review includes first-person recollection of1970sgraduate/early-career scholarship and names Davis prominently within a plural cohort. It supports an attributed scholarly resource, not sole mentoring, a fixed school, or a claim that every part of Faust’s work derives from Davis. Her later discussion is a review of Davis2014, not fresh reading of the trilogy.
primary_locators: The Scholar Who Shaped History, opening scholarly-revolution/For me recollection and ensuing Davis intellectual-history paragraph; later PSAR ideals/social-action discussion.

proposals.relationship: Davis adapts Freudian transference, through Erikson’s Gandhi’s Truth, as one explanation for metropolitan British concern with distant slavery.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by Manisha Sinha (2019), p. 151/n. 25: she identifies Davis’s admiration for Erik H. Erikson’s 1969 book and his application of transference in Age of Revolution. Erikson retains the intermediary credit; no direct Freud reading or whole-book method is asserted. Sinha criticizes this psychological explanation; Foner separately criticizes a later Freudian excursion, without documenting the same transmission chain. Freud, Erikson and Davis originals remain unread.
primary_locators: Sinha 2019 printed p. 151, first two paragraphs and n. 25 (citing Davis’s Age of Revolution pp. 18, 350, 379); Foner 2014 paragraph beginning What interests Davis, however, is less the legal.
